content:
The letter arrived in a cream envelope thick enough to imply money.

I distrusted it immediately.

Toph distrusted all envelopes on principle.

Katara distrusted the seal.

Aang distrusted nothing until he read the first page.

Then he went very still.

We were eating breakfast in the courtyard. Toph had one foot hooked around the leg of my chair. Katara was sorting clinic appointment slips. I was pretending not to sort them for her. Aang had been halfway through a steamed bun when the messenger arrived.

“What?” Katara asked.

He handed her the letter.

She read.

Her mouth flattened.

Toph held out a hand. “Somebody translate the rich-person threat paper for the blind woman.”

I took the second page.

It was not exactly a threat.

That almost made it worse.

A coalition of donors supporting Air Nomad cultural restoration wanted to fund a new temple complex outside Cranefish Town. Housing. Archives. Schools. Gardens. A sanctuary for sky bison.

All good things.

Then came the conditions.

The board wanted Aang to appoint a hereditary council to “ensure the continuity of authentic Air Nomad bloodlines.” It suggested that his future children should hold ceremonial authority and that “appropriate household arrangements” ought to be considered in light of his responsibility as the last surviving Air Nomad.

The letter never named Katara.

It did not name Toph.

It definitely did not name me.

It treated us as variables surrounding Aang’s body.

For several seconds, nobody spoke.

Then Toph said, “I can eat it.”

Katara looked at her.

“The letter,” Toph clarified. “Not the donors. Probably.”

Aang stood.

“I need air.”

Nobody pointed out that air was everywhere.

He left through the gate.

Katara started after him.

Then stopped.

Her hand closed into a fist at her side.

“I hate this.”

“So does he,” I said.

“I know.”

“No. I mean he hates being followed when he needs to think.”

Katara looked toward the gate.

Years of loving someone had taught her when care meant pursuit and when it meant waiting.

She sat back down.

Toph reached for the letter.

I gave it to her.

She tore it exactly in half.

Katara said, “We may need that.”

“For what?”

“Evidence.”

Toph sighed and handed me the pieces. “Paperwork can heal it.”

“I am not a waterbender for documents.”

“You kind of are.”

I spent the morning angry at people I had never met.

Not because they cared about Air Nomad survival.

Aang cared about it more than anyone alive.

Because they had turned that grief into a claim.

A claim on his future. His children. Our relationships. Katara’s body, perhaps, though they were polite enough not to write that part down.

At noon, Aang returned.

His face was calm.

That did not mean he was calm.

“I’m going to meet them,” he said.

Katara stood. “Not alone.”

“I know.”

He looked at all three of us.

“I want you there.”

Toph cracked her knuckles.

“Emotionally,” Aang added.

“No promises.”

The donors received us in a rented council chamber three days later.

Six people sat behind a long table. Two were Air Acolytes. Three were wealthy merchants. One was an Earth Kingdom scholar who had written extensively about Air Nomad history and, judging from Aang’s expression, had occasionally explained that history to Aang himself.

Bad choice.

The chairman began warmly.

“Avatar Aang, our only wish is preservation.”

Aang folded his hands.

“Mine too.”

Encouraged, the man continued. “Then you understand why continuity requires planning. Your generation carries obligations no ordinary household would bear.”

Toph’s foot tapped once against the stone floor.

Katara spoke before she could.

“Our household is not yours to plan.”

The chairman smiled in the careful way people did when they wanted to dismiss Katara without appearing to dismiss a war hero.

“Master Katara, no disrespect is intended.”

“Then respect us.”

I loved her a little painfully in that moment.

A scholar cleared his throat. “Historically, communal family structures among Air Nomads—”

Aang lifted one hand.

The room stopped.

“Historically,” he said, “children were raised communally in temples. Air Nomads did not build dynasties.”

The scholar blinked.

Aang’s voice stayed gentle.

“My people valued freedom from attachment to status and possession. You are proposing that my children inherit authority because of blood.”

“We are proposing stability.”

“You are proposing a monarchy with arrows.”

Toph made a choking sound beside me.

Katara looked down to hide a smile.

The chairman’s face reddened.

Aang did not.

That was one of the ways people underestimated him. They mistook kindness for softness. They mistook refusal to dominate for inability to stand firm.

Toph had taught him earthbending years ago.

Sometimes I could still see the lesson in him.

He planted himself.

“If I have children,” Aang said, “they will be people. Not cultural property.”

My stomach tightened.

“If Katara has children, if Toph has children, if my partner has children, if any of us do or do not have children, those choices belong to the people making them.”

He did not look at me while he said it.

I was grateful.

The room suddenly felt too aware of bodies and possibilities.

One donor leaned forward. “Avatar, surely you feel some obligation to restore what was lost.”

Aang’s expression changed.

For the first time, anger showed.

“I was twelve when my people were murdered.”

No one moved.

“I woke up and everyone I had ever known was dead. I have spent every year since then being told I owe the world a solution to that.”

His voice did not rise.

It became quieter.

“There is no solution.”

The words were terrible because they were true.

“I can protect what remains. I can teach. I can rebuild traditions honestly. I can support Air Acolytes. I can protect sacred places. I can raise children, if I choose to have them, with knowledge of where they come from.”

His hands flattened against the table.

“But I cannot make genocide unhappen by producing descendants.”

Katara’s eyes shone.

Toph’s jaw tightened.

I wanted to touch him.

I did not.

This was his ground to hold.

Aang looked at the proposed contract in front of him.

“I will accept funds for a school, archives, gardens, and bison sanctuary with public oversight and no hereditary authority.”

The chairman inhaled.

Aang continued. “Or I will build it slowly without you.”

That was the end of the meeting.

Not officially.

There were another forty minutes of negotiation.

But it was the end in every way that mattered.

Outside, Toph waited until the doors closed.

Then she punched Aang lightly in the shoulder.

“Ow.”

“That was for ‘monarchy with arrows.’”

“You liked that.”

“I loved it. That’s why you get hit.”

Katara wrapped both arms around him.

This time he let her.

His face disappeared into her shoulder.

I stood near them, suddenly unsure.

Aang reached one hand out without looking.

I took it.

Toph pressed her shoulder against his back.

Four people in a government hallway, holding one another badly.

After a while, Aang pulled away.

“I meant what I said.”

Katara brushed at the corner of one eye. “About what?”

“Children.”

The air shifted.

Toph groaned. “Can we not turn trauma into a family-planning meeting?”

Aang laughed, shaky and grateful.

“No. Not now.”

He looked at me.

“I just don’t ever want you to think I see you as a possibility for something I need from your body.”

My throat tightened.

The rough draft of us—the one I had carried privately before reality made it better—had contained exactly that fear. That I might be valuable because I was a nonbender, because I represented some chance, some future, some answer to a loss too large for any family to repair.

I squeezed his hand.

“Thank you.”

Toph tilted her head. “For the record, anyone who tries to assign reproductive duties in our house is getting launched into the canal.”

Katara said, “Toph.”

“What? I didn’t say from how high.”

Aang laughed again.

This time, so did I.

That night we climbed onto our roof.

Aang lay flat on his back, looking at stars none of us could see the same way.

Katara rested against his shoulder. Toph lay with one foot touching mine. I watched clouds move over the moon.

“Roots and wings,” Aang said.

Toph groaned. “Here comes the poetry.”

“I’m serious.”

“That’s worse.”

Aang ignored her.

“I used to think rebuilding meant making things the way they were.”

Katara traced a circle against his sleeve.

“And now?” she asked.

“Now I think roots are what tell you where you came from.” He smiled faintly. “Wings are what let you become something your ancestors didn’t have to imagine.”

Toph was quiet.

Then: “Still poetry.”

“Good poetry?”

“No.”

I reached across the roof and found his hand in the dark.

He did not need to restore an extinct world by turning us into instruments of it.

We could help him remember.

We could help him build.

We could love the living man without demanding that he become a monument to the dead.

For that night, it was enough.
